name: William IV
role: King of the United Kingdom (1830–1837); earlier naval officer and Duke of Clarence
summary: A naval officer turned king whose recorded political stance is thin and mostly conservative. As Duke of Clarence he spoke in the Lords against limiting the slave trade, citing West India property, and later he accepted the Whigs and the Reform Act only reluctantly, resisting mass creation of peers. In 1834 he dismissed the Melbourne ministry, partly over fears of radicalism and Church reform.

notes: Thin record: a naval officer-prince whose political voice is the 1799 Lords speech and his acts as king. Reform Act 1832, abolition of slavery 1833 and Poor Law 1834 are not counted as his positions (assent on ministers' advice). Wikipedia reports other remarks (support for Catholic emancipation and for relief of dissenters, opposition to the 1800 adultery remarriage bar, dislike of interference in other states' affairs, assent to the 1833 Hanover constitution) but its footnotes were not traced to a primary text, so they are not used. Themes searched: government, society, world, liberty, economy; nothing further answers the other statements. This pass nulled five earlier answers (see their reviewHistory).
